title: Greek and Latin roots
blurb: Use the core Greek and Latin roots to unlock unfamiliar words, including the look-alikes and double meanings the TEAS likes to test.
question: A TEAS item asks what "manuscript" originally meant. You have never studied the word, but you know two roots inside it. How do roots let you work out the meaning, and which look-alike roots could trip you up?

teach.h: The root carries the core meaning
teach.body: Formally, a root is the base of a word that carries its core meaning; prefixes and suffixes attach to it, sometimes with a combining vowel. In plain English: the root is what the word is really about. Many English words share Greek and Latin roots, so learning one root unlocks a whole family: dict (say) gives predict, dictate and contradict.

teach.caption: A prescription is written before the medicine is given. The root gives the core: writing.
When a root has two meanings, let the rest of the word and the sentence decide.

items: Strip off any prefix and suffix to find the root.
Think of a word you already know with the same root (vis: visible, video).
Add back the prefix and suffix: they turn and label the meaning.
Check every part of your chosen answer against every part of the word.
Confirm the meaning fits the sentence.

teach.body: Tanya Brooks, preparing for a radiography program, reads that some nerve damage is 'irreversible.' She finds the root vers (turn), the prefix ir- (not), the prefix re- (back) and the suffix -ible (able to be). Put together: not able to be turned back. She rejects 'easily turned around' because ir- means not, and 'broken beyond repair' because the root is vers (turn), not rupt or fract (break).

teach.text: Two TEAS traps. First, an option that matches ONE part of the word but contradicts another: for 'transport,' 'pulled across' matches trans- but uses tract (pull), not port (carry). Second, roots with two meanings: ped is foot in 'pedal' but child in 'pediatric.' Synonym roots also appear: rupt and fract both mean break; scrib/script and graph/gram both mean write.

items: The root carries the core meaning; prefixes and suffixes modify and label it.
Senses: aud hear, vis/vid see, spec look, sens feel, phon sound.
Actions: port carry, tract pull, duct lead, ject throw, mit send, rupt/fract break, vert turn.
Life and time: bio life, viv/vit live, mort death, chron time, cred believe.
ped = foot or child; path = feeling or disease: use context.

summary: You can now recognize the core Greek and Latin roots and use them to work out unfamiliar words. You can also handle roots with two meanings, spot synonym roots, and reject options that match only part of a word.

A.why: Aud means hear, so audible means able to be heard.

whyNot.2: Speak is dict or voc (dictate, vocal).

A.q: Which word contains a root meaning "carry"?
A.why: Port means carry, so transport means to carry across.

whyNot.0: Mit means send: transmit means to send across.
whyNot.1: Tract means pull: traction is a pulling force.
whyNot.3: Scrib means write: transcribe means to write across into another form.

A.q: Based on its root, events listed in "chronological" order are arranged by
A.why: Chron means time, so chronological order follows the sequence in time.

whyNot.0: Size has no connection to chron.
whyNot.1: Order of importance is a different organizing pattern; chron refers to time.
whyNot.2: Order by location is spatial order; chron refers to time.

B.q: Which word means "able to be believed"?
B.why: Cred means believe and -ible means able to be: credible means able to be believed.

whyNot.0: Vers means turn: reversible means able to be turned back.
whyNot.2: Aud means hear: audible means able to be heard.
whyNot.3: Frag means break: fragile means easily broken.

B.q: A pediatric clinic treats patients who are
B.why: In pediatric, ped means child, so a pediatric clinic treats children.

whyNot.0: Ped can mean foot (pedal), but in medical words like pediatric it means child; foot care is podiatry.
whyNot.1: Older adults relate to ger or geront, not ped.
whyNot.2: The mind is psych, not ped.

B.q: Which pair of roots share the same meaning?
B.why: Rupt (rupture) and fract (fracture) both mean break.

whyNot.0: Port means carry and tract means pull.
whyNot.1: Spec means look and sens means feel.
whyNot.3: Mit means send and junct means join.

C.q: Read the sentence: "The nurse told the patient to avoid heavy lifting that could cause the healing incision to rupture." Based on its root, "rupture" most nearly means
C.why: Rupt means break, so to rupture is to break or burst open, which fits a warning about a healing incision.

whyNot.1: Swelling is not breaking; nothing in rupt means to enlarge.
whyNot.2: A color change has no link to rupt (break).
whyNot.3: Closing over is the opposite of breaking open.

C.q: Which word contains a root that means "turn"?
C.why: Vers means turn, so reverse means to turn back.

whyNot.0: Vit means live: vital means necessary for life.
whyNot.2: Viv means live: vivid means full of life.
whyNot.3: Vis means see: visible means able to be seen.

C.q: Using its word parts, a "manuscript" was originally a document that was
C.why: Manu means hand and script means write: a manuscript was written by hand.

whyNot.0: Reading aloud would involve a voice root such as voc or dict.
whyNot.1: Far is tele and send is mit; neither root appears in manuscript.
whyNot.3: Manu (hand) contradicts a machine; this matches script but ignores manu.

reteach.title: A root is a family name
reteach.question: Think of a big family that shares one last name. How does a root work like that surname across many words?

blocks.body: Everyone in the Dict family has something to do with saying: Predict says before, Dictate says aloud for someone to write, Contradict says against. The first names (prefixes) and job titles (suffixes) differ, but the surname tells you the family business. Meet a stranger called 'Dictum' and you can already guess it involves saying something.

blocks.text: Some families share a first letter but not a surname: vit and viv mean live, vis means see and vers means turn. Read the whole root, not just its first two letters.

explain.body: aud hear, vid/vis see, spec/spect look, sens/sent feel, phon sound, man/manu hand, ped/pod foot, corp body, psych mind, cogn know.

test.q: Based on its root, a "spectator" at a hospital fundraiser is someone who
test.why: Spect means look, and -or names a person who does something: a spectator is a person who watches.

whyNot.1: Speaking would be dict or voc, not spect.
whyNot.3: Writing is scrib/script or graph, not spect.

explain.body: duc/duct lead, port carry, tract pull, ject throw, mit/mis send, rupt and fract/frag break, sect cut, junct join, struct build, scrib/script and graph/gram write, dict say, vert/vers turn.

test.q: Based on its word parts, "inject" means to
test.why: In- here means into and ject means throw: to inject is to throw or force into.

whyNot.0: Pull is tract (traction), and in- here means into, not out of.
whyNot.1: Send is mit and across is trans- (transmit).

explain.body: bio life, viv/vit live, mort death, chron time, therm heat, hydr water, photo light, tele far, bene good, phil love, cred believe, log/logy word or study of.

test.q: Based on its root, a hospital's "mortality" rate counts
test.why: Mort means death, so a mortality rate counts deaths.

whyNot.0: Births have nothing to do with mort; it means death.
whyNot.2: Illness relates to path (disease), not mort.
whyNot.3: Mort means death; an injury is not a death.

explain.body: Some roots carry two meanings: ped can be foot (pedal) or child (pediatric); path can be feeling (empathy) or disease (pathology). Let the rest of the word and the sentence decide.

test.q: In which word does path mean "feeling" rather than "disease"?
test.why: Empathy is sharing another person's feelings, so path here means feeling.

whyNot.0: Pathology is the study of disease.
whyNot.1: Neuropathy is disease of the nerves.
